title: Callbacks
text:
Callbacks
Each callback below computes one variable per area. MaxCB, MinCB, StdCB, CountCB and MoranICB return NaN for an area without measurements. A missing count is therefore NaN, not 0. Optimizer.get_rank treats a missing value as the highest priority for its criterion.
To add a variable, subclass Callback and implement __call__(loc_id, o). Return a tuple of Variables to add several columns at once.


source

MaxCB
def MaxCB(
    name:str='Max', # Name of the variable
):
Highest measured value in the area. NaN if the area has no measurements.




source

MinCB
def MinCB(
    name:str='Min', # Name of the variable
):
Lowest measured value in the area. NaN if the area has no measurements.




source

StdCB
def StdCB(
    name:str='Standard Deviation', # Name of the variable
):
Standard deviation of the measured values in the area. NaN if the area has no measurements.




source

CountCB
def CountCB(
    name:str='Count', # Name of the variable
):
Number of measurements in the area. NaN if the area has no measurements.




source

MoranICB
def MoranICB(
    k:int=5, # Number of neighbours per point, used to expand the measurements and to build the spatial weights
    p_threshold:float=0.05, # Significance level: Moran's I is `NaN` when its pseudo p-value `p_sim` is at or above it
    name:str='Moran.I', # Name of the variable
    min_n:int=5, # Areas with `min_n` measurements or fewer get `NaN`
):
Moran’s I of the area’s measurements and their nearest neighbours. NaN if the area has too few measurements or Moran’s I is not significant.




source

PriorCB
def PriorCB(
    fname_raster:str, # Raster used as the prior
    name:str='Prior', # Name of the variable
):
Mean of fname_raster over the area, emulating prior knowledge such as an airborne survey. Computed for every area, measured or not.

title: Callbacks
text:
Example
The example emulates one campaign on a 10 by 10 grid. Each area gets between 0 and 9 points:

fname_raster = 'files/ground-truth-01-4326-simulated.tif'
gdf_grid = gridder(fname_raster, nrows=10, ncols=10)
n = np.random.default_rng(41).integers(0, 10, size=len(gdf_grid))
samples_t0 = DataCollector(fname_raster).collect(Sampler(gdf_grid).sample(n, method='uniform', rng=41))


ax = samples_t0.plot(column='value', s=3, legend=True)
gdf_grid.boundary.plot(color=black, lw=0.5, ax=ax)
ax.axis('off');








Create a State with the callbacks to compute, then call it to get one row per area. MoranICB tests significance with random permutations. Fixing NumPy’s global seed makes its results reproducible:

np.random.seed(0)
state = State(samples_t0, gdf_grid, cbs=[
    MaxCB(), MinCB(), StdCB(), CountCB(), MoranICB(k=5), PriorCB(fname_raster)
])
state_t0 = state()
test_eq(len(state_t0), len(gdf_grid))

get computes the variables of one area:

[Variable(name='Max', value=np.float32(0.16029228)),
 Variable(name='Min', value=np.float32(0.11158965)),

Expanding measurements for Moran’s I
Moran’s I measures spatial autocorrelation. It is close to 1 when nearby measurements have similar values, and close to 0 when values are spatially random. One area rarely has enough measurements to estimate it alone. MoranICB therefore adds the k nearest measurements of each point in the area, including those in neighbouring areas. expand_to_k_nearest does this expansion.
The plot shows the expanded measurements of the area with the most measurements, and the areas they come from:

loc_id = state_t0['Count'].idxmax()
subset = state.measurements.loc[[loc_id]]
expanded_pts = state.expand_to_k_nearest(subset, k=5)
test_eq(len(expanded_pts), 5 * len(subset))
ax = expanded_pts.plot(column='value', s=10, legend=True)
gpd.sjoin(gdf_grid, expanded_pts, how="inner", predicate='contains').boundary.plot(color=black, lw=0.5, ax=ax)
ax.axis('off');

title: Run a campaign over several years
text:
This guide runs a sampling campaign over several years with the same budget each year. The first year ranks the areas from prior knowledge alone. Each later year ranks them from all the measurements collected so far, with the six state variables and weights of Round II in Getting started.
Each year, rank_to_sample with the quantiles policy splits the budget across four quartiles of areas by rank. The first quartile shares 50% of the budget, the second 30%, the third 20% and the last none. min=1 raises every area to at least one sample. The total can then exceed the budget.
crumbs: Run a campaign over several years

title: Run a campaign over several years
text:
Set up the area

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd

from trufl.utils import gridder
from trufl.sampler import Sampler, rank_to_sample
from trufl.collector import DataCollector
from trufl.callbacks import State, MaxCB, MinCB, StdCB, CountCB, MoranICB, PriorCB
from trufl.optimizer import Optimizer

As in the tutorial, the simulated contamination map is the ground truth. A 10 x 10 grid over it gives the administrative units:

fname_raster = '../files/ground-truth-01-4326-simulated.tif'
gdf_grid = gridder(fname_raster, nrows=10, ncols=10)
sampler = Sampler(gdf_grid)
dc_emulator = DataCollector(fname_raster)
crumbs: Run a campaign over several years

title: Run a campaign over several years
text:
Set the campaign parameters

number_of_years = 4
yearly_sample_budget = 150
benefit_criteria = [True, True, True, False, False, True]
weights = [0.2, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2]

The criteria and weights apply to the state variables in the order of the callbacks: maximum, minimum, standard deviation, sample count, Moran’s I and prior.
crumbs: Run a campaign over several years

title: Run a campaign over several years
section: Rank the areas for the first year
text:
Rank the areas for the first year
Before any measurement, the state holds only the prior:

samples_t0 = gpd.GeoDataFrame(index=pd.Index([], name='loc_id'), geometry=None, data={'value': None})
state_t0 = State(samples_t0, gdf_grid, cbs=[PriorCB(fname_raster)])()
df_rank = Optimizer(state=state_t0).get_rank(is_benefit_x=[True], w_vector=[1],
                                             n_method=None, c_method=None, w_method=None, s_method="CP")
crumbs: Run a campaign over several years

title: Run a campaign over several years
text:
Sample and re-rank every year
Each year, sample the areas according to the current ranking, add the measurements to those collected so far, then rank the areas again from the new state. Each panel shows the ranking used that year, with all samples so far:

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, number_of_years, figsize=(12, 4))
samples = []
for year, ax in enumerate(axs, start=1):
    n = rank_to_sample(df_rank['rank'].sort_index().values, budget=yearly_sample_budget, min=1, policy="quantiles")
    samples.append(dc_emulator.collect(sampler.sample(n, method='uniform')))
    samples_sofar = pd.concat(samples)

    gdf_grid.join(df_rank).plot(column='rank', cmap='Reds_r', ax=ax)
    samples_sofar.plot(column='value', cmap='viridis', s=1, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"Year {year} ({len(samples_sofar)} samples)")
    ax.axis('off')

    state = State(samples_sofar, gdf_grid, cbs=[
        MaxCB(), MinCB(), StdCB(), CountCB(), MoranICB(k=5), PriorCB(fname_raster)])
    df_rank = Optimizer(state=state()).get_rank(is_benefit_x=benefit_criteria, w_vector=weights,
                                                n_method="LINEAR1", c_method=None, w_method=None, s_method="CP")
plt.tight_layout()
crumbs: Run a campaign over several years

def reproject_raster(
    src_fname:str, # Path to the source GeoTIFF

)->None:

Resampling uses the nearest neighbour. Each output cell copies the value of the closest input cell, and no values are interpolated.

title: Getting started
text:
In this tutorial you plan two sampling rounds over a simulated map of soil contamination. The map is the ground truth. You emulate each field measurement by reading the value of the map at the sample location.
You work through these steps:

title: Getting started
text:
Imports

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import rasterio
import geopandas as gpd

from trufl.utils import gridder
from trufl.sampler import Sampler, rank_to_sample
from trufl.collector import DataCollector
from trufl.callbacks import (State, MaxCB, MinCB, StdCB, CountCB, MoranICB, PriorCB)
from trufl.optimizer import Optimizer


red, black = '#BF360C', '#263238'

Our simulated ground truth
The assumed ground truth reveals a typical spatial pattern of contaminant such as Cs137 after a nuclear accident for instance:

title: Getting started
section: Round I: Optimize sampling based on prior at \(t_0\)
text:
Round I: Optimize sampling based on prior at \(t_0\)

What prior knowledge do we have?
At the initial time \(t_0\), data sampling has not yet begun, but we can often leverage existing prior knowledge of our phenomenon of interest to inform our sampling strategy/policy. In the context of nuclear remediation, this prior knowledge can often be obtained through mobile surveys, such as airborne or carborne surveys, which can provide a coarse estimation of soil contamination levels.
In the example below, we simulate prior information about the soil property of interest by calculating the average value of the property over each grid cell.
At this stage, we have no measurements, so we simply create an empty Geopandas GeoDataFrame.

samples_t0 = gpd.GeoDataFrame(index=pd.Index([], name='loc_id'), 
                              geometry=None, data={'value': None})







Tip



We need to set an index loc_id and have a geometry and value columns.


Now we get/“sense” the state of our grid cells based on the simulated prior (Mean over each grid cell PriorCB):

state = State(samples_t0, gdf_grid, cbs=[PriorCB(fname_raster)])

# You have to call the instance

title: Getting started
section: Round II: Optimize sampling with additional insights at \(t_1\)
text:
Round II: Optimize sampling with additional insights at \(t_1\)
For each administrative unit, we now have additional knowledge acquired during the previous campaign, in addition to our prior knowledge. In the current round, the optimization of the sampling will be carried out based on the maximum, minimum, standard Deviation, number of measurements already conducted, our prior knowledge, and an estimate of the presence of spatial trends or spatial correlations (Moran’s I).






Tip



It’s worth noting that you can use any quantitative or qualitative secondary geographical information as a variable in the state, such as population, whether any previous remediation actions have taken place, the economic impact of the contamination, and so on.

Tip



The Moran’s I index is a statistical method used to determine if there is a spatial correlation/trend within each area of interest. For example, a random field would have a Moran’s I index close to 0, while a clear gradient of low to high values, such as from south to north, would be characterized by a Moran’s I index close to 1.




Finding optimal number of samples to be collected

We first decide if each variable of the State are to maximize (benefit) or minimize (cost):


benefit_criteria = [True, True, True, False, False, True]


Then assign an importance weight to each of the variable of the State (Min, Max, …):


optimizer = Optimizer(state=state())
df_rank = optimizer.get_rank(is_benefit_x=benefit_criteria,

title: Trufl
text:
Trufl helps you decide where to sample next in a survey that runs over several rounds. At each round, it ranks areas, such as administrative units, by how much they need more samples. It then splits your sampling budget across the areas according to their rank. The ranking uses multiple-criteria decision-making (MCDM) on criteria that you choose, computed from the measurements collected so far and from prior knowledge such as an airborne survey.
Trufl was built to plan soil surveys of farmland contaminated after a nuclear accident. The same approach works for any phenomenon you monitor over time against several criteria, such as legacy contaminants.
trufl is part of the ecosystem of DSS4NAFA, a decision support system for nuclear emergencies affecting food and agriculture. Where trufl comes from describes the research behind trufl and how it works with DSS4NAFA.

title: Trufl
text:
Why trufl
Sampling theory and the research literature already cover multi-stage and adaptive spatial sampling well. Their methods rest on assumptions, such as a planned probability sampling design or a known model of spatial variation. In a nuclear emergency, the data rarely meet those assumptions. Measurements arrive over time from many sources, such as airborne surveys, laboratory analyses and samples taken where it was convenient to take them. They cover different locations at different resolutions. Sound statistical inference from such data is difficult. Decisions still have to be made, and you can’t ignore the data you have. trufl takes a pragmatic approach and uses all of it.
The reasons to sample one area before another also vary, and they change during an emergency. They include the levels measured so far, the uncertainty that remains, prior knowledge, land use and population. trufl ranks areas on criteria that you choose, with weights that you set. You can change both from one round to the next.
Like DSS4NAFA, trufl is not a black box. Each rank follows from the state of the area, the criteria, the weights and the scoring method. You can inspect each of them, and adjust them as the situation develops.
You can also use trufl to prepare for an emergency. Simulate a campaign over several rounds on a map of a possible contamination, and compare sampling strategies before you need them.

title: Trufl
text:
Install
pip install trufl

title: Trufl
text:
Example
This example plans one sampling round over a simulated contamination map, split into a 10 x 10 grid of areas:

import pandas as pd
import geopandas as gpd

from trufl.utils import gridder
from trufl.callbacks import State, PriorCB
from trufl.optimizer import Optimizer
from trufl.sampler import Sampler, rank_to_sample


fname_raster = './files/ground-truth-01-4326-simulated.tif'
gdf_grid = gridder(fname_raster, nrows=10, ncols=10)

Before any measurement, the state of each area is its prior: the mean of the map over the area. Calling a State computes it:

no_samples = gpd.GeoDataFrame(index=pd.Index([], name='loc_id'), geometry=None, data={'value': None})
state = State(no_samples, gdf_grid, cbs=[PriorCB(fname_raster)])()

title: Trufl
text:
Documentation

Getting started runs two sampling rounds on the simulated map, with plots.
Run a campaign over several years re-ranks and resamples the areas every year with a fixed budget.
Where trufl comes from describes the research behind trufl and its place in the DSS4NAFA ecosystem.
How trufl ranks areas explains the criteria, weights and scoring methods.
The API reference documents each module.

title: Trufl
text:
Acknowledgements
trufl started within the IAEA Coordinated Research Project D15019, “Monitoring and Predicting Radionuclide Uptake and Dynamics for Optimizing Remediation of Radioactive Contamination in Agriculture”, led by the Joint FAO/IAEA Centre of Nuclear Techniques in Food and Agriculture. It is actively maintained.
It builds on the PhD research of Floris Abrams at SCK CEN and KU Leuven. Floris Abrams and Franck Albinet wrote the package. Where trufl comes from describes the research and how trufl works with DSS4NAFA.

title: Where trufl comes from
text:
DSS4NAFA is a decision support system for nuclear emergencies affecting food and agriculture. The Joint FAO/IAEA Centre of Nuclear Techniques in Food and Agriculture led its development through two IAEA Coordinated Research Projects (CRPs):

D15015, Response to Nuclear Emergencies Affecting Food and Agriculture, from 2013 to 2019.
D15019, Monitoring and Predicting Radionuclide Uptake and Dynamics for Optimizing Remediation of Radioactive Contamination in Agriculture. trufl started within this CRP.

After a release of radionuclides, food and health authorities use DSS4NAFA to manage data on contaminated soil and crops. It also advises them on sampling and plans the sampling campaigns.
The DSS4NAFA video shows the system. Lee Zhi Yi and Dercon (2019) describe the data management and visualisation approach behind it.

title: Where trufl comes from
text:
How trufl fits in
trufl adds adaptive sampling strategies to the sampling plans of DSS4NAFA. At each round, trufl ranks the areas by sampling need from the measurements collected so far, then splits the sampling budget across them. How trufl ranks areas explains the ranking.
DSS4NAFA imports a sampling plan as a CSV file with one row per sample location.

title: Where trufl comes from
text:
Research context
trufl draws on the PhD research of Floris Abrams at KU Leuven and SCK CEN (Abrams, 2023). The thesis develops tools for deciding where, how and when to remediate agricultural land after a large-scale release of radionuclides. It applies them to two agricultural watersheds: the Maarkebeek in Flanders, Belgium, and the Niida in Fukushima Prefecture, Japan.
trufl also draws on OREFA, an unpublished toolbox from the same research.

title: MCDM
text:
The functions in this module turn a decision matrix into a ranking. Each row of the matrix is an alternative, such as an area to sample, and each column is a criterion. Ranking takes three steps:
Optimizer.get_rank runs the three steps. Every step takes its method as a name, such as LINEAR2 or TOPSIS, in any case.
The functions use these parameter names throughout:
This module adapts code from mcdm, Copyright (c) 2020-2022 Dimitrios-Georgios Akestoridis, released under the MIT License.

title: MCDM
text:

Each method checks its inputs first and raises ValueError if they do not suit it.

title: MCDM
text:
Normalization
Normalization rescales each criterion so that criteria measured in different units can be compared. LINEAR1 and LINEAR2 also turn every cost criterion into a benefit criterion.


source

linear1
def linear1(
    x_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Decision matrix
    is_benefit_x:list, # Benefit (`True`) or cost (`False`) flag of each criterion
)->tuple: # The normalized matrix and the new benefit flags, `(z_matrix, is_benefit_z)`
Divide each benefit criterion by its maximum, and the minimum of each cost criterion by its values. Every criterion becomes a benefit criterion.




source

linear2
def linear2(
    x_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Decision matrix
    is_benefit_x:list, # Benefit (`True`) or cost (`False`) flag of each criterion
)->tuple: # The normalized matrix and the new benefit flags, `(z_matrix, is_benefit_z)`
Rescale each criterion to [0, 1] between its minimum and maximum, reversed for cost criteria. Every criterion becomes a benefit criterion.




source

linear3
def linear3(
    x_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Decision matrix
    is_benefit_x:list, # Benefit (`True`) or cost (`False`) flag of each criterion
)->tuple: # The normalized matrix and the new benefit flags, `(z_matrix, is_benefit_z)`
Divide each criterion by its sum. Benefit and cost flags are unchanged.




source

vector
def vector(
    x_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Decision matrix
    is_benefit_x:list, # Benefit (`True`) or cost (`False`) flag of each criterion
)->tuple: # The normalized matrix and the new benefit flags, `(z_matrix, is_benefit_z)`
Divide each criterion by its Euclidean norm. Benefit and cost flags are unchanged.




source

normalize
def normalize(
    x_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Decision matrix
    is_benefit_x:list, # Benefit (`True`) or cost (`False`) flag of each criterion
    n_method:str, # `LINEAR1`, `LINEAR2`, `LINEAR3`, `VECTOR`, or `None` to keep a matrix already in [0, 1]
)->tuple: # The normalized matrix and the new benefit flags, `(z_matrix, is_benefit_z)`
Normalize x_matrix with n_method.


The examples below use three areas and three criteria: the highest measured value, the number of measurements and a prior estimate. The number of measurements is a cost criterion, because areas with fewer measurements need more sampling:

x = np.array([[0.8, 4, 0.5],
              [0.3, 2, 0.9],
              [0.6, 8, 0.2]])
is_benefit_x = [True, False, True]

LINEAR2 maps the lowest value of each criterion to 0 and the highest to 1. It reverses the scale of the cost criterion. Area 2 has the most measurements and gets 0:

z, is_benefit_z = normalize(x, is_benefit_x, 'LINEAR2')
test_eq(is_benefit_z, [True, True, True])
test_close(z[:, 1], [2/3, 1, 0])
z

array([[1.        , 0.66666667, 0.42857143],
       [0.        , 1.        , 1.        ],
       [0.6       , 0.        , 0.        ]])


Missing values stay NaN. Each normalizer computes its column statistics from the values that are present. A missing value does not change how the rest of its column is normalized:

x_gap = np.array([[2.,  10.],
                  [4., np.nan],
                  [8.,   5.]])
z_gap, _ = normalize(x_gap, [True, False], 'LINEAR1')
test_close(z_gap[[0, 2]], [[0.25, 0.5], [1., 1.]])
test_eq(np.isnan(z_gap[1, 1]), True)
z_gap

array([[0.25, 0.5 ],
       [0.5 ,  nan],
       [1.  , 1.  ]])

title: MCDM
MCDM
text:
Weighting
Weighting methods derive the importance of each criterion from the data. Every method returns weights that sum to 1.


source

em
def em(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix whose columns each sum to 1, as `LINEAR3` produces
)->numpy.ndarray:
Criterion weights from the Entropy Measure (EM) method.




source

mw
def mw(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix
)->numpy.ndarray:
Equal weights for every criterion, from the Mean Weights (MW) method.




source

sd
def sd(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix
)->numpy.ndarray:
Criterion weights proportional to the standard deviation of each column, from the Standard Deviation (SD) method.




source

vic
def vic(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix
    c_method:str='dCor', # `ABSPEARSON` or `DCOR`. `None` means `DCOR`
)->numpy.ndarray:
Criterion weights from the Variability and Interdependencies of Criteria (VIC) method.




source

critic
def critic(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix
    c_method:str='Pearson', # `PEARSON`, `ABSPEARSON` or `DCOR`. `None` means `PEARSON`
)->numpy.ndarray:
Criterion weights from the Criteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation (CRITIC) method.




source

weigh
def weigh(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix
    w_method:str, # `MW`, `EM`, `SD`, `CRITIC` or `VIC`
    c_method:str=None, # Correlation method for `CRITIC` and `VIC`
)->numpy.ndarray:
Criterion weights of z_matrix, computed with w_method.


MW gives every criterion the same weight. CRITIC gives more weight to criteria that vary more and correlate less with the others. Here it gives the first criterion almost half of the total weight:

test_close(weigh(z, 'MW'), [1/3, 1/3, 1/3])
w = weigh(z, 'CRITIC', 'PEARSON')
test_close(w.sum(), 1)
w

array([0.4931945 , 0.23714979, 0.26965571])

title: MCDM
text:
Scoring
Scoring methods combine the normalized criteria and their weights into one score per alternative.


source

topsis
def topsis(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix
    w_vector:list, # Weight of each criterion
    is_benefit_z:list, # Benefit (`True`) or cost (`False`) flag of each criterion
)->tuple: # The scores and `True`, as `(s_vector, desc_order)`
Score each alternative by its relative closeness to the ideal alternative, from 0 to 1, with the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS). Higher is better.




source

cp
def cp(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix
    w_vector:list, # Weight of each criterion
    is_benefit_z:list, # Benefit (`True`) or cost (`False`) flag of each criterion
)->tuple: # The scores and `False`, as `(s_vector, desc_order)`
Score each alternative by its Euclidean distance to the ideal alternative, with Compromise Programming (CP). Lower is better.




source

score
def score(
    z_matrix:<built-in function array>, # Normalized decision matrix
    is_benefit_z:list, # Benefit (`True`) or cost (`False`) flag of each criterion
    w_vector:list, # Weight of each criterion
    s_method:str, # `CP` or `TOPSIS`
)->tuple: # The scores, and `True` if higher scores rank first, as `(s_vector, desc_order)`
Score each alternative of z_matrix with s_method.


score returns the scores and desc_order. desc_order is True when higher scores rank first. TOPSIS ranks area 0 first, then area 1, then area 2:

s_topsis, desc_order = score(z, is_benefit_z, w, 'TOPSIS')
test_eq(desc_order, True)
test_eq(np.argsort(-s_topsis), [0, 1, 2])
s_topsis

array([0.75394406, 0.42133458, 0.41935961])


CP also ranks area 0 first, but it ranks area 2 above area 1. Lower CP scores rank first:

s_cp, desc_order = score(z, is_benefit_z, w, 'CP')
test_eq(desc_order, False)
test_eq(np.argsort(s_cp), [0, 2, 1])
s_cp

array([0.17318287, 0.4931945 , 0.40972278])

title: Optimizer
text:
Optimizer decides where the next sampling campaign matters most. It takes the state of each location, one row per loc_id and one column per criterion, as returned by calling a State (see trufl.callbacks). get_rank normalizes the criteria, weighs them and scores each location with the functions in trufl.mcdm. Rank 1 is the location that most needs more samples. rank_to_sample in trufl.sampler turns these ranks into a number of samples per location.


source

Optimizer
def Optimizer(
    state:pandas.DataFrame, # One row per `loc_id` and one column per criterion, as returned by calling a `State`
):
Rank locations by sampling priority from their state variables.




source

Optimizer.get_rank
def get_rank(
    is_benefit_x:list, # One flag per criterion: `True` if a high value raises sampling priority (benefit), `False` if a low value does (cost)
    w_vector:list=None, # Weight of each criterion, summing to 1, or `None` to compute weights with `w_method`
    n_method:str=None, # Normalization method: `LINEAR1`, `LINEAR2`, `LINEAR3`, `VECTOR`, or `None` for values already in [0, 1]
    c_method:str=None, # Correlation method for `CRITIC` and `VIC` weighting: `PEARSON`, `ABSPEARSON` or `DCOR`
    w_method:str=None, # Weighting method used when `w_vector` is `None`: `MW`, `EM`, `SD`, `CRITIC` or `VIC`
    s_method:str=None, # Scoring method: `CP` or `TOPSIS`. Required
)->pandas.DataFrame: # A `rank` column indexed by `loc_id`, sorted from highest priority (rank 1) to lowest
Rank each location in state by sampling priority.


The examples below use three locations and two criteria. Max is the highest value measured at a location, and Count is how many measurements it has. Location 2 has no measurements yet, so its Max is missing:

state = pd.DataFrame({'Max': [0.8, 0.3, np.nan], 'Count': [4, 2, 0]},
                     index=pd.Index([0, 1, 2], name='loc_id'))
opt = Optimizer(state)

Max is a benefit criterion, because a high value raises priority. Count is a cost criterion, because a high value lowers priority. Both criteria get the same weight here. CP (compromise programming) scores each location by its distance to an ideal location that has the best value of every criterion:

ranks = opt.get_rank(is_benefit_x=[True, False], w_vector=[0.5, 0.5], n_method='LINEAR2', s_method='CP')
test_eq(ranks['rank'].to_dict(), {2: 1, 0: 2, 1: 3})
ranks








rank


loc_id





2
1


0
2


1
3







A missing value counts as the highest priority for its criterion. Location 2 ranks first because it has no measurements. Location 0 ranks above location 1 because its Max is higher.
Leave out w_vector to compute the weights from the data with w_method. MW (mean weights) gives every criterion the same weight, and it reproduces the ranking above:

test_eq(opt.get_rank(is_benefit_x=[True, False], n_method='LINEAR2', w_method='MW', s_method='CP'), ranks)

title: How trufl ranks areas
text:
trufl ranks areas by sampling priority with multiple-criteria decision-making (MCDM). It scores each area against criteria and weights that you choose, then ranks the areas by score. Rank 1 is the highest sampling priority. Why trufl explains why trufl takes this approach.
The examples on this page use the six criteria and weights of Round II in Getting started, on a state table of four areas small enough to read in full.
import pandas as pd
from fastcore.test import test_eq
from trufl.optimizer import Optimizer
from trufl.sampler import rank_to_sample

title: How trufl ranks areas
text:
Criteria
Each column of the state that a State returns is one criterion. You choose the columns through the callbacks you pass to State. Round II uses these six:



Criterion
Callback
Type




Maximum sample value
MaxCB()
Benefit


Minimum sample value
MinCB()
Benefit


Standard deviation
StdCB()
Benefit


Sample count
CountCB()
Cost


Moran’s I
MoranICB(k=5)
Cost


Prior estimate
PriorCB()
Benefit



A high value of a benefit criterion raises the priority of an area. A low value of a cost criterion raises it. In Round II, an area with few samples therefore ranks higher than a well-sampled one. An area whose values show no spatial trend, with a Moran’s I close to 0, ranks higher than one with a clear gradient, with a Moran’s I close to 1.
The state can hold any other quantitative variable as a criterion, such as population or whether an area has been remediated.
Here is a state for four areas. Areas 0 and 1 have high values, but area 0 has two samples and area 1 has twelve. Areas 2 and 3 have low values, with three and ten samples:

state = pd.DataFrame({'Max': [9.0, 9.5, 3.0, 2.5], 'Min': [2.0, 1.5, 0.5, 1.0],
                      'Standard Deviation': [2.5, 2.0, 0.8, 0.3], 'Count': [2, 12, 3, 10],
                      'Moran.I': [0.1, 0.6, 0.2, 0.7], 'Prior': [6.0, 7.0, 2.0, 1.5]},

title: How trufl ranks areas
text:
Weights
The weight vector sets the importance of each criterion relative to the others. The weights must sum to 1. If you pass w_vector=None, get_rank computes the weights from the data with w_method instead. mcdm describes the weighting methods.
With the Round II weights, area 0 ranks first. Area 1 has similar values but many more samples, and ranks second:

optimizer = Optimizer(state)
ranks = optimizer.get_rank(is_benefit_x=is_benefit, w_vector=[0.2, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2],
                           n_method='LINEAR1', s_method='CP')
test_eq(ranks['rank'].to_dict(), {0: 1, 1: 2, 2: 3, 3: 4})

title: How trufl ranks areas
text:
Normalization
The criteria have different units and ranges, such as a number of samples and a contamination level. Before scoring, get_rank rescales every criterion with n_method. Round II uses LINEAR1. It divides each benefit criterion by its maximum, and divides the minimum of each cost criterion by its values. Every criterion then lies in [0, 1], and a higher value always means a higher priority. mcdm describes the other normalization methods.

title: How trufl ranks areas
text:
Scoring: CP and TOPSIS
Both scoring methods compare each area with the ideal area, which has the best value of every criterion. Compromise programming (CP) scores each area by its weighted distance to the ideal area. The lowest score ranks first. TOPSIS also measures the distance to the worst possible area. It scores each area by its relative closeness to the ideal area, from 0 to 1. The highest score ranks first.
With the Round II weights, both methods rank the four areas in the same order. With the count-heavy weights, they disagree on the last place. TOPSIS ranks area 1 third and area 3 last:

ranks = optimizer.get_rank(is_benefit_x=is_benefit, w_vector=count_heavy, n_method='LINEAR1', s_method='TOPSIS')
test_eq(ranks['rank'].to_dict(), {0: 1, 2: 2, 1: 3, 3: 4})
ranks








rank


loc_id





0
1


2
2


1
3


3
4

title: How trufl ranks areas
text:
From ranks to sample counts
rank_to_sample turns the ranks into a number of samples for each area. It takes the ranks in loc_id order. The default Weighted policy gives each area a share of the budget proportional to 1/rank. For the TOPSIS ranks above and a budget of 20 samples:

ranks_by_loc = ranks['rank'].sort_index().values
rank_to_sample(ranks_by_loc, budget=20)

array([10,  3,  5,  2])


The quantiles policy, which the tutorial uses, splits the areas into four quartiles by rank. The first quartile shares 50% of the budget, the second 30%, the third 20% and the last none. With four areas, each quartile holds one area:

rank_to_sample(ranks_by_loc, budget=20, policy='quantiles')

array([10,  4,  6,  0])


sampler describes both policies and the min parameter.

title: Data Collector
text:
source

DataCollector
def DataCollector(
    fname_raster:str, # Path to the raster used as ground truth
    band:int=1, # Band to read
):
Emulate field measurements by reading a raster at sample locations.




source

DataCollector.get_values

DataCollector.collect
def collect(
    gdf:geopandas.geodataframe.GeoDataFrame, # Sample locations as `Point` or `MultiPoint` geometries, indexed by `loc_id`
)->geopandas.geodataframe.GeoDataFrame: # One `Point` per row with its measured `value`, indexed by `loc_id`
Measure the raster at every point of gdf.


DataCollector stands in for a real field campaign. It treats a raster as the ground truth and reads the value under each sample location. Use it to test a sampling strategy before collecting real data. The example starts with a 10 by 10 grid over the raster:

fname_raster = './files/ground-truth-01-4326-simulated.tif'
gdf_grid = gridder(fname_raster, nrows=10, ncols=10)

Draw between 1 and 9 points in each grid cell:

sampler = Sampler(gdf_grid)
n = np.random.default_rng(0).integers(1, 10, size=len(gdf_grid))
sample_locs = sampler.sample(n, method='uniform', rng=0)

collect splits each MultiPoint into single points and reads the raster under each one. The result has one row per measurement. loc_id repeats for areas with several points:

dc_emulator = DataCollector(fname_raster)
samples_t0 = dc_emulator.collect(sample_locs)
test_eq(len(samples_t0), n.sum())

rank_to_sample
def rank_to_sample(
    ranks:numpy.ndarray, # Rank of each area, in `loc_id` order. Rank 1 is the highest priority
    budget:int, # Total number of samples to allocate
    min:int=0, # Minimum number of samples per area
    policy:str='Weighted', # Allocation policy: `Weighted` or `quantiles`
)->numpy.ndarray: # Number of samples for each area, in the order of `ranks`
Split budget samples across areas according to their ranks.


rank_to_sample connects Optimizer.get_rank to Sampler.sample. It turns each area’s rank into the number of points to draw there. The examples below use 8 areas ranked from 1 to 8 and a budget of 80 samples:

ranks = np.arange(1, 9)

The Weighted policy gives each area a share of the budget proportional to 1/rank, rounded to the nearest integer:

n = rank_to_sample(ranks, budget=80)
test_eq(n, [29, 15, 10, 7, 6, 5, 4, 4])
n

array([29, 15, 10,  7,  6,  5,  4,  4])


The quantiles policy splits the areas into four quartiles by rank. The first quartile shares 50% of the budget, the second 30%, the third 20% and the last none:

n = rank_to_sample(ranks, budget=80, policy='quantiles')
test_eq(n, [20, 20, 12, 12, 8, 8, 0, 0])
n

array([20, 20, 12, 12,  8,  8,  0,  0])


min raises every area to at least that many samples. The total can then exceed budget, because rank_to_sample does not take the extra samples from other areas. Rounding can also make the total differ slightly from budget:

test_eq(rank_to_sample(ranks, budget=80, min=1, policy='quantiles').sum(), 82)
